output.risk_summary: Taking Advil and Aleve together is unsafe and provides no extra pain relief. This combination significantly increases your risk of stomach bleeding, ulcers, and kidney damage.

details.finding: Combining two NSAIDs (ibuprofen in Advil and naproxen in Aleve)
details.explanation: Both Advil and Aleve are anti-inflammatory painkillers called NSAIDs. Taking them together does not relieve pain any better than taking just one, but it does make stomach bleeding, ulcers, and kidney damage much more likely. NSAIDs work the same way in your body, so doubling up creates serious harm without any benefit.

details.finding: Naproxen sodium dose exceeds safe limit
details.explanation: You are taking 880 mg of naproxen sodium per day from Aleve, but the safe over-the-counter limit is 660 mg per day. Taking more than this increases the risk of stomach problems, bleeding, and kidney damage.

output.what_to_do: Stop taking both products together immediately. Choose only one painkiller. If you need pain relief throughout the day, use either Advil (ibuprofen) or Aleve (naproxen), but never both. For Aleve specifically, do not exceed three pills (660 mg) in 24 hours. If one NSAID is not controlling your pain adequately, do not add a second one on your own. Instead, you can alternate an NSAID with acetaminophen (Tylenol), which works differently and is safe to combine with either ibuprofen or naproxen. Always take NSAIDs with food to protect your stomach.
